body:
Cities generate both waste and recoverable resources

Urban activities generate food waste, packaging, discarded products, sewage and construction debris. If these materials are mixed and discarded without proper management, they can pollute land and water, obstruct drains and increase the demand for disposal space.

A circular urban system attempts to reduce waste generation and recover useful resources before final disposal. This requires action by households, commercial establishments, waste collectors, processing facilities and urban local bodies.

Source segregation under the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026

The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026 were notified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on 27 January 2026 and came into force on 1 April 2026. They superseded the Solid Waste Management Rules, 2016, subject to the transitional provisions in the notification.

Rule 5 requires waste generators to segregate and store solid waste at source in 4 separate streams: wet waste, dry waste, sanitary waste and special care waste.

Waste streamTypical contentsAppropriate management approach
Wet wasteFood and other suitable biodegradable organic wasteComposting, biomethanation or other appropriate biological processing
Dry wasteRecyclable and non-recyclable dry materialsSorting, suitable material recycling and appropriate management of rejects
Sanitary wasteUsed sanitary pads, diapers and similar wasteSeparate collection and appropriate treatment under applicable requirements
Special care wasteCertain household items requiring special handling, such as discarded paint containers, lamps and expired medicinesSeparate collection and channelisation to suitable authorised facilities

The dry-waste category includes both recyclable and non-recyclable material. Dry waste must therefore be sorted further before deciding whether it can be recycled, used in another permitted recovery process or safely disposed of.

The rules separately address construction and demolition waste and require its management according to the relevant specialised rules. Industrial hazardous waste, biomedical waste, electronic waste, battery waste and radioactive waste remain subject to their respective regulatory frameworks rather than being treated as ordinary municipal solid waste.

Material Recovery Facilities

A Material Recovery Facility (MRF) receives and sorts suitable waste, particularly dry materials, so that recoverable fractions can be channelled to appropriate recyclers.

An MRF is different from an STP or an ETP. An MRF is concerned mainly with sorting and recovery of solid materials, whereas sewage and effluent treatment plants manage wastewater.

Segregation at the source improves the usefulness of recyclable materials because it reduces contamination by food residues and other unsuitable waste.

Organic waste, compost and biogas

Biodegradable organic waste can be processed in different ways. Composting converts suitable organic matter into a more stable product that may be used as a soil amendment when it meets applicable quality requirements.

Biomethanation, or anaerobic digestion, breaks down suitable organic material without oxygen and produces biogas. The gas contains methane and can provide useful energy when appropriately collected and used.

Composting and biomethanation should not be confused with the recovery of metal or plastic. They are methods of managing biodegradable organic resources.

Urban wastewater as a resource

Cities also support circularity by treating sewage and supplying reclaimed water for appropriate uses. Surat's treated-wastewater projects demonstrate this connection between municipal services and industrial demand.

Urban resource management is therefore broader than solid-waste collection. It includes water supply, sewage treatment, material recovery, organic-waste processing and controlled management of unusable residues.

Why implementation matters

A city may collect waste but still recover little value if segregation is poor. A waste-processing facility can also create environmental problems if its rejects, odours, leachate or emissions are not adequately managed.

Effective circular management requires separate collection, suitable processing capacity, trained workers, reliable end users for recovered materials and continued environmental monitoring.

Prelims focus

  • The Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, came into force on 1 April 2026.
  • The rules specify 4 source-segregation streams: wet, dry, sanitary and special care waste.
  • Dry waste may contain both recyclable and non-recyclable fractions.
  • MRF means Material Recovery Facility.
  • Composting processes suitable organic waste, while biomethanation produces biogas.
  • Trap: The 2026 municipal solid-waste framework does not replace the separate rules governing industrial hazardous waste or electronic waste.

[Sources: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, S.O. 388(E), dated 27 January 2026, rules 1–5 and definitions of wet waste, dry waste, sanitary waste, special care waste, composting and biomethanation, consulted 2 November 2026; Surat Municipal Corporation, Action Plan: Reuse and Recycle of Treated Wastewater, 2019, pp. 4–6; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 166–172.]

title: Circular Resource Management in Gujarat's Cities

body:
Why several institutions are involved

Gujarat's circular-economy opportunities involve industrial development, municipal services, pollution regulation and coastal management. No single institution performs all these functions.

Understanding the responsibilities of the main organisations helps distinguish infrastructure development from environmental regulation and resource-efficiency promotion.

Principal institutions and their functions

InstitutionPrincipal role relevant to this topicTypical connection
GIDCDevelopment and organisation of industrial estates and supporting infrastructureIndustrial areas, water and drainage infrastructure, shared facilities
GCPCPromotion of cleaner production and resource-efficient industrial practicesAwareness, assessment and demonstration of waste-reduction measures
Gujarat Pollution Control Board (GPCB)State-level pollution prevention and control under applicable environmental lawsIndustrial pollution regulation, consent and applicable authorisations
Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)National pollution-control functions, standards and technical guidance under applicable lawsWaste-management guidelines and regulatory coordination
Urban local bodiesMunicipal solid-waste and sewage services within their jurisdictionsCollection, segregation, treatment and reuse projects
Gujarat Maritime BoardState maritime infrastructure and environmental management functions within its remitNon-major ports and Alang–Sosiya ship recycling

The Gujarat Cleaner Production Centre has promoted cleaner production since 1998. Its activities have included awareness programmes and cleaner-production assessments in industrial sectors.

Pollution control boards and industrial development organisations perform different functions. GIDC may provide or support industrial infrastructure, while environmental approvals and pollution-control obligations arise under the applicable regulatory framework.

How a resource-efficiency project can be implemented

A successful project begins by identifying the resource being used, the waste being generated and the possible safe alternatives. It must then demonstrate that the proposed recovery or reuse route is practical and environmentally appropriate.

  1. Identify the resource problem. Determine whether excessive water use, material loss, energy consumption or waste generation is the main concern.
  2. Prioritise prevention. Reduce avoidable consumption and waste generation before considering treatment or recovery.
  3. Identify compatible uses. Match a recoverable resource to a suitable user. Treated wastewater, for example, must meet the requirements of its intended use.
  4. Provide necessary infrastructure. Arrange suitable collection, storage, transport, treatment or distribution facilities.
  5. Apply environmental safeguards. Follow applicable rules, authorisations and quality requirements, including proper management of hazardous residues.
  6. Check the actual result. Assess whether the project reduces fresh resource consumption and pollution without creating greater environmental burdens elsewhere.

Practical opportunities in Gujarat

Industrial clusters: Shared treatment facilities and appropriate exchange of recoverable materials can reduce duplicated infrastructure and resource losses. Chemical-industry clusters require particular attention to wastewater quality and hazardous-waste controls.

Water-stressed urban and industrial areas: Treated municipal wastewater can supply suitable industrial and other non-potable uses, provided it meets applicable quality requirements. Surat offers a documented example of this approach.

Cities: Segregating waste at source makes material recovery and biological processing more effective. Municipalities can also link sewage treatment with suitable water-reuse projects.

Ports and coastal areas: Reusable equipment, suitable scrap and other recoverable materials can be retained in productive use. Ship recycling requires separate handling of hazardous residues and protection of the coastal environment.

Suitable residual waste: Material that cannot be appropriately reused or recycled may be assessed for permitted recovery, including co-processing where technically suitable and legally authorised.

How to distinguish the main interventions

Consider 3 different situations. First, a factory reduces the amount of water required to manufacture the same quantity of goods. That is resource efficiency. Second, a factory uses suitably treated municipal wastewater instead of fresh water. That is water reuse. Third, several factories send compatible wastewater to a common treatment plant. That is shared effluent treatment.

The 3 activities can support a circular economy, but they are not identical. A common treatment plant may discharge treated water without reusing it. Similarly, a recycling facility may recover material without reducing pollution unless its operations are properly managed.

Limits of circular-economy measures

Resource recovery cannot be evaluated solely by the quantity of material processed. Important considerations include the quality of recovered resources, energy consumed, emissions generated, risks to workers and the environment, and the need for final disposal of remaining residues.

For example, wastewater reuse may reduce freshwater withdrawals but still require energy for treatment and pumping. Recycling contaminated materials may create dangerous residues. Co-processing may substitute some conventional inputs but still requires emission control.

Thus, the central objective is not simply to increase the number of recycling projects. It is to achieve measurable and environmentally sound reductions in resource use, waste and pollution.

Prelims focus

  • GIDC develops industrial estates; GCPC promotes cleaner production; GPCB regulates pollution under applicable laws.
  • Surat's wastewater reuse provides an example of linking municipal treatment with industrial water demand.
  • Alang–Sosiya illustrates material recovery through ship recycling together with the need for hazardous-waste management.
  • Waste prevention, reuse, recycling, recovery and disposal represent different levels of the waste-management hierarchy.
  • Trap: The presence of treatment infrastructure, the existence of a policy target and the achievement of a circular-economy outcome are 3 separate matters.

[Sources: Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation, Plug and Play facilities in GIDC and Useful Links, consulted 2 November 2026; Gujarat Cleaner Production Centre, Objectives, including establishment and cleaner-production functions, consulted 2 November 2026; Gujarat Maritime Board, Environment FAQs and Ship Recycling Yards, consulted 2 November 2026; Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, Solid Waste Management Rules, 2026, rules 2–5; Surat Municipal Corporation, Action Plan: Reuse and Recycle of Treated Wastewater, 2019, pp. 4–6; NCERT, Class 11, Indian Economic Development, chapter 9, Environment and Sustainable Development, printed pp. 164–172.]
